WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — Costs of Running a Restaurant
WorkedExamples.Question: An original soup recipe for 8 servings needs 1.2 kg vegetable A at $3/kg and 0.8 kg vegetable B at $4.50/kg. Calculate ingredient cost per serving and write cell formulas that would recalculate if servings changed.
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: Ingredient A cost 1.2×3=$3.60 and B cost 0.8×4.50=$3.60.
A spreadsheet can store amounts B2/B3, unit costs C2/C3, servings F1 and use D2=B2*C2, D3=B3*C3, total SUM(D2:D3), per serving=SUM(D2:D3)/F1.
Change F1 to 6 and verify per-serving cost becomes $1.20 if batch quantities remain the same.
WorkedExamples.Answer: $7.20 per batch, $0.90 for 8 servings, $1.20 for 6 servings at same batch size.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks an actual working spreadsheet with appropriately referenced cells and genuinely sourced ingredient costs if used for a real menu.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — More Costs of Running a Restaurant
WorkedExamples.Question: An original café sells 800 meals at $9 each, food costs $3 per meal, and ongoing fixed expenses are $2,800/month. Compute monthly profit and break-even meal count.
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: Food cost is 800×$3=$2,400; adding fixed expenses gives $5,200 costs.
Contribution margin is $9−$3=$6/meal; break-even fixed/$6=$2,800/$6≈466.67, so at least 467 whole meals.
WorkedExamples.Answer: $2,000 profit at 800 meals; break-even 467 whole meals under the stated assumptions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews independently proposed fixed versus per-meal costs, relevant missing expenses and a clear budget ledger.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — Measurement Error (Part 1)
WorkedExamples.Question: One board measures 10.0 cm to the nearest tenth. The true length can lie from 9.95 cm (inclusive) to just below 10.05 cm. Give the largest possible relative error measured against the actual length.
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: A rounding to nearest 0.1 cm implies error magnitude no greater than about 0.05 cm.
At the lower actual bound 9.95 cm, relative error can be 0.05/9.95≈0.005025.
Express this as about 0.503% of actual length; at the upper side the denominator is larger.
Draw a scale/ruler reading and state endpoint conventions before presenting a strict largest value.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Maximum relative error approximately 0.503%, with endpoint interpretation depending on rounding ties.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks original physical ruler/uncertainty interval and correct percent denominator.

Independently authored educational tasks using historical OUR/IM Grade 7 source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/9/9/preparation.html (2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 lineage); publisher images/assessments not reproduced.

This optional integrated project builds on earlier Grade 7 mathematics and distinguishes computed illustrative answers from authentic student investigations. Teacher review is required for original designs, unit choices, physical measurements, assumptions and written justification; no numeric answer alone constitutes academic acceptance.

Publisher student lesson reviewed: Propagate measurement error through area and volume multiplicatively. First-party task below is an independent numerical and representation model, NOT a record of real ingredient prices, field measurements, student surveys, spreadsheet operations or trundle-wheel construction. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/9/9/index.html. Project completion requires real artifacts, teacher rubric and genuine evidence; do not auto-approve an arithmetic result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — Measurement Error (Part 2)
WorkedExamples.Question: Two sides of a rectangle are independently measured 5% HIGH, so measured length and width each equal 1.05 times actual. What is the resulting area percent error? Extend to three dimensions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: If all three dimensions are 5% HIGH, measured volume factor=1.05³=1.157625.
Volume is 15.7625% HIGH; clearly distinguish worst-direction assumptions and dimension units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Area +10.25% and volume +15.7625% under all-dimensions-5%-high assumptions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks labeled measured-vs-true shapes and interpretation; this is not a blanket bound for all rounding outcomes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming area error equals the length error without accounting for multiplication.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It confuses assumptions, units or the mathematical model needed to complete the project.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Document sources and derive each output from correctly identified measures.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Presenting a correct illustrative calculation as a complete authentic project
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lesson assesses an actual constructed, measured or justified student artifact.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require a teacher rubric for original solutions, precision and communication.

SummaryPoints: Area products inherit errors in each measured length.
A small difference in side length can produce a larger change in computed area.
State interval or estimate rather than false exactness.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — Measuring Long Distances Over Uneven Terrain
WorkedExamples.Question: An original marked trail is measured twice by pacing at 612 m and 600 m, and another method returns 606 m. What might be reported, and how far are the first estimates apart as a percent of the 606 m comparator?
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: Record three labeled measurements: 612,600,606 m; identify methods and uncertainties.
Difference between first two is 12 m.
Relative to explicitly chosen 606 m comparator, 12/606×100≈1.98%.
Propose reporting around 606 m with a stated uncertainty, not a false exact distance; teacher should review the chosen comparator.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Difference 12 m, about 1.98% of the 606 m comparison value.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks actual repeated measurements and methodological notes; hypothetical data do not certify fieldwork.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original project task — Designing a 5K Course
WorkedExamples.Question: An original school walk plan uses a measured loop of 1,250 m with a safe start/finish area. How many whole loops make 5 km, and what map evidence must a student supply before organizers approve it?
WorkedExamples.Method: Document assumptions and units, build the source-relevant spreadsheet, measurement apparatus, scale drawing, sampling table or proposal, then submit a teacher-reviewed artifact.
Steps: Draw loop route, start/finish position, safe crossings and direction arrows on an original scale map.
Use at least two authentic wheel measurements per route and revise if measurements differ; share a teacher-reviewed proposal.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Four 1,250 m laps make 5 km in the model, pending real route measurement.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher-only rubric: field measurement, repeated trials, accurate map/scale, physical safety, coherent revision and organizer-ready presentation.
